opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually less likely to come from the place everyone expects, which is the fully general humanoid that walks into your kitchen and does your laundry. That's the long-term vision, and I'm excited about it, but the hardware is still expensive, the reliability isn't there yet, and honestly people are a bit nervous about having a 70-kilo machine moving around their kids and their pets.

Where I see the opening is in something smaller, cheaper, and more open — almost like the early days of personal computing. Think about what made the iPhone work: it wasn't that it did one thing perfectly, it was that it became a platform. Developers could build on it, and suddenly you had thousands of use cases nobody at Apple had imagined. I think robotics needs that moment, where the robot is affordable enough — a few hundred dollars, not tens of thousands — that hobbyists, students, tinkerers can actually own one and program it.

That's part of why we've been so invested in open-source robotics at Hugging Face, with LeRobot and the small desktop robots. When you put a robot on someone's desk and connect it to a community that's sharing datasets, sharing trained policies, sharing apps, you get this flywheel. Someone teaches it to sort Lego, someone else teaches it to water plants, someone builds a little companion that reacts to you while you code. Individually these sound like toys. Collectively, that's how you discover what people actually want robots to do.

And the other piece is that AI has changed the equation. Before, every behavior had to be hand-engineered. Now, with vision-language-action models, you can show the robot a task a few dozen times, or even just describe it, and it generalizes. So the software is finally catching up to where the "app store" model becomes possible.

So if I had to bet: the iPhone moment is a cheap, friendly, hackable robot, probably not humanoid at first, with an open ecosystem around it. The humanoids will come, but they'll stand on the data and the community that the smaller robots build first.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, when I think about the iPhone moment, I think people often misunderstand what it actually was. The iPhone wasn't the first smartphone, it wasn't the first touchscreen, it wasn't the first device with a camera and a browser. What it did was take a bunch of components that had finally become good enough and cheap enough, and wrap them in something that felt obvious the moment you held it. And crucially, it opened a platform where thousands of other people could build the things Apple never would have thought of.

So if you map that onto robotics, I'd say the opening is not where most people are looking. Everyone is obsessed with the humanoid form factor, and I understand why, it's a very compelling image, but I think the humanoid is more like the Newton than the iPhone. It's trying to do everything at once, in a body that's still extremely expensive and hard to make reliable, before the software is really there.

What I find much more promising is the convergence of three things that have quietly become good enough. First, the vision-language-action models. For the first time you can give a robot a natural instruction and have it generalize somewhat to objects and situations it hasn't seen in training. That's genuinely new, that was science fiction three or four years ago. Second, the hardware has gotten dramatically cheaper. You can now build a capable manipulator arm for a few hundred dollars, with off-the-shelf servos and 3D-printed parts. And third, which is the part I care most about, there's now an open ecosystem forming around all of this. Open models, open datasets, open hardware designs, where a student in their bedroom can download a policy, fine-tune it on an afternoon of teleoperation data, and have something working.

So my bet is that the iPhone moment doesn't come from one company shipping one miraculous product. It comes from a cheap, relatively simple device, maybe an arm, maybe a small wheeled base with an arm, maybe something that sits on your kitchen counter, that is just good enough at a narrow set of boring tasks that people actually want done. Folding laundry, loading the dishwasher, tidying up. Tasks that are not glamorous, but where "pretty good" is already valuable. And then the platform effect kicks in. Because the models are open and the hardware is accessible, you get a long tail of people teaching these things new skills and sharing them, the way the App Store unlocked the iPhone.

If I had to pick one lesson from the history of these moments, it's that the magic was never in the hardware alone. It was in making the hardware a surface that a whole community could build on. And robotics is just now reaching the point where that community can exist. That's the opening.

astra-6.text:
I think the home is probably the most interesting place, but I’m not sure the entry point is a humanoid robot that does everything. It might be something much narrower: a robot that does one useful thing reliably enough that you actually want to live with it.

For me, the promising opening is teaching. Today, you largely buy a robot for the tasks somebody has programmed into it. If you could show it something—“Here’s how I want you to put these things away”—and it could learn that from a few demonstrations, that would change the relationship quite a lot. You’re buying something you can adapt to your own life.

The hard part is making that work in an ordinary home, with all the variation and unexpected situations. But if someone gets that interaction right, makes it reliable and affordable, I could imagine that being the moment when people suddenly understand why they want a robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the home is probably the most interesting place, but I’m not convinced the first breakthrough will be a humanoid that does everything. It might be a robot that does one thing you really want to stop doing, and does it reliably enough that you stop thinking about it.

For me, the interesting question is how quickly it can learn your particular environment. Every kitchen is different, every home is different. If you need an engineer to come and set it up, it’s very hard to make that a consumer product. If you can show it what you want, correct it a few times, and it improves, then you have something much more compelling.

So I would look for a useful task, a price people can afford, and that ability to adapt. The “iPhone moment” might be when those come together, rather than when we first see a very impressive robot demo.
